2025.note: Larson took a second title in the strangest way available to him: a right-front tyre problem put him a lap down, a caution on lap 221 gave him the wave-around, and from fifth on the final restart he finished third — enough, because the highest finisher of the four is champion. He won three races that year, at Homestead, Bristol and Kansas.

2024.note: Logano’s third title came from a season in which he was not the dominant driver: Ryan Blaney finished second in the standings, William Byron third and Tyler Reddick, the regular-season champion, fourth. Under the elimination format a regular season counts for nothing once the Championship 4 line up level at Phoenix.

2023.note: Blaney won his first championship ahead of Kyle Larson, William Byron and Christopher Bell, giving Team Penske back-to-back titles after Logano’s the year before.

2022.note: Logano took a second title ahead of Ross Chastain, Christopher Bell and Chase Elliott — Elliott having won the regular-season championship and finished fourth of the four, which is the format in miniature. It was the debut season of the Next Gen car, delayed a year by the pandemic, and one of the most open in the series’ history: nineteen different drivers won a race, matching the modern-era record set in 2001.

2021.note: Larson started the finale from pole, led 107 laps and won the race for the tenth time that season, which settled his first championship. It closed a season that began with him out of the sport: he had been suspended indefinitely in April 2020 for using a racial slur during an online race, completed sensitivity training, and was reinstated on 1 January 2021 before signing for Hendrick Motorsports.

2020.clinched: Phoenix, 8 November 2020, in the Championship 4 finale
2020.note: Elliott won the Season Finale 500 and the championship ahead of Brad Keselowski, Joey Logano and Denny Hamlin. The season had been broken in half by the pandemic and resumed in May with no practice and no qualifying at all, drivers going straight from the transporter to the green flag. His father Bill Elliott had been champion before him.

2019.clinched: Homestead-Miami, 17 November 2019, in the Championship 4 finale
2019.note: Busch won the last race to take his second title, five points clear of Martin Truex Jr. with Kevin Harvick seven back and Denny Hamlin thirteen. He had won four of the first fourteen races and then gone twenty-one without a victory before finding it again when it counted.

2018.note: Logano won his first title by winning the race, passing Martin Truex Jr. on the high side with twelve laps to go. He had won three races all season.

2017.note: Truex Jr. won the championship five points clear of Kyle Busch and seven clear of Kevin Harvick, and did it for Furniture Row Racing, a small operation out of Denver that had only become a two-car team that year. He was regular-season champion as well. 2017 was also the first season of stage racing, most races split into three stages with points at the end of each.

2016.note: Johnson’s seventh title tied Richard Petty and Dale Earnhardt for the most anyone has won. Joey Logano finished three points behind him, the defending champion Kyle Busch five behind and Carl Edwards 33 — margins that look impossibly tight because the Championship 4 start the last race level.

2015.clinched: Homestead-Miami, 22 November 2015, in the Championship 4 finale
2015.note: Busch won his first championship having missed the first third of the season with severe leg injuries. Kevin Harvick was runner-up, Jeff Gordon five points back and Martin Truex Jr. eleven. Under the old points system a driver who missed eleven races could not have won; under the elimination playoff he could.

2014.clinched: Homestead-Miami, 2014, in the first Championship 4 finale
2014.note: Harvick won the first championship under the elimination format, in the year it was introduced: sixteen drivers, four rounds, the four lowest-scoring eliminated after each of the first three, and a final four who start the last race on level points with the highest finisher taking the title. He drove for Stewart-Haas Racing, the team co-owned by the 2011 champion.

2013.note: Johnson finished ninth in the last race to take a sixth title, 28 points clear of Matt Kenseth, with six race wins. It was the last championship decided under the original Chase before the elimination format arrived.

2012.note: Keselowski finished fifteenth in the closing race, which was enough as points leader, and won by 39 points from Clint Bowyer with Jimmie Johnson a point further back. He took five races that year — Bristol, Talladega, Kentucky, Dover and the Chase opener at Chicagoland — in a Dodge, and gave Roger Penske his first Cup championship.

2011.clinched: Homestead-Miami, 20 November 2011, tied on points and settled on race wins
2011.note: Stewart won the final race with Carl Edwards second, and the two finished the season level on points. The title went to Stewart on the tiebreak of victories, five to one, all five of his coming during the Chase. He was also the car’s owner, the first owner-driver champion since Alan Kulwicki in 1992.

2010.note: Johnson passed Denny Hamlin in the points during the closing race to take a fifth consecutive title, with six race wins. No driver has won five in a row before or since.

2009.season: a fourth consecutive title in 2009, and seven race wins
2009.note: Johnson became the only driver to win four championships back to back, a record that stood until he extended it himself the following year.

2008.season: a third consecutive title in 2008, and seven race wins
2008.note: Johnson became the second driver in the series’ history to win three championships in a row.

2007.note: Johnson won ten races, more than in any other of his championship seasons, and took a second consecutive title.

2006.note: Johnson’s first title came from eighth in the Chase standings, turned around by five consecutive top-two finishes including a win at Martinsville. He won five races that year, and nine more championships would follow for Hendrick Motorsports drivers over the next fifteen seasons.

2005.note: Stewart took a second championship having locked up the number one seed for the Chase by winning at Indianapolis, the track nearest his home. He won five races that year, at Sonoma, Daytona, New Hampshire, Watkins Glen and Indianapolis.

2004.note: Kurt Busch won the first championship decided by a playoff, by eight points from Jimmie Johnson with Jeff Gordon third, sixteen back. The Chase had been introduced that season: the top ten after race 26, plus anyone within 400 points of the leader, had their scores reset to five points apart and ten races to settle it. He drove a Ford for Roush Racing.

2003.season: the 2003 season, won with a single race victory — and it changed the sport
2003.note: Kenseth won one race all year, at Las Vegas in the third round, and beat Jimmie Johnson to the championship by 90 points with Dale Earnhardt Jr. third. He led the standings for 33 consecutive weeks, a series record, and after the Coca-Cola 600 his lead reached 160 points and never fell below it across the remaining 24 races. NASCAR created the Chase for the following season primarily because of it: a champion could be crowned with a month to spare and one win to his name.

2002.season: the 2002 season, and a first title
2002.note: Stewart won four races — Atlanta, Richmond, Watkins Glen and Indianapolis — and held off Mark Martin to take the championship in his last season driving a Pontiac. Five years earlier he had won the IndyCar title, and he remains the only driver to have won championships in both.

2001.season: the 2001 season, which began with the death of Dale Earnhardt
2001.note: Gordon won a fourth championship in seven years, 349 points clear of Tony Stewart. The season had opened with the Daytona 500 on 18 February, where Earnhardt, a seven-time champion, was killed on the last lap: he misjudged a block on Sterling Marlin, got loose off Marlin’s right front, overcorrected into Ken Schrader and hit the turn four wall, dying instantly of a basilar skull fracture. Safety changes followed across the sport, and crowds began holding three fingers up on the third lap.

2000.season: the 2000 season, decided over a full year rather than a playoff
2000.note: Labonte won the championship for Joe Gibbs Racing by 265 points from Dale Earnhardt, with Jeff Burton third, taking wins including Rockingham and Indianapolis. It was the last full-season points title before the format began changing, and Earnhardt, the runner-up, would be killed in the opening race of the following season.
